scenes.narration: Last time, the challenge was to print 1 to 50 with a while loop. Start i at 1, while i is at most 50, print i and a space, then i plus plus. And print the newline after the loop. Did you get it? Now look at this. The start, the check and the update were spread over three lines. Today we squeeze all three into one line.

scenes.onScreen: `for (init; condition; update)` with three labelled boxes and arrows showing run order 1→2→body→3→2…
scenes.animation: Numbers pop onto each part in order; arrow loops 3 times
scenes.narration: A for loop has three parts inside the round brackets, separated by semicolons. First, the init: int i equals 1. This runs only once, at the very start. Second, the condition: i less than or equal to 5. This is checked before every iteration. Third, the update: i plus plus. This runs after every iteration, at the end of the body. So the order is: init, check, body, update, check, body, update, and so on, until the check is false. It's like planning a trip: where you start, where you stop, and how big each step is. All on one line, before you even begin.

scenes.animation: Bus icon moves stop to stop for loop 1; `sum` tracker climbs to 55; countdown digits shrink
scenes.narration: Let's read three for loops. [HL 4] Line four: for, int i equals 1, i less than or equal to 5, i plus plus. The variable i is created right here, inside the for. [TRACK i=1] [HL 5] Line five prints "Bus stop" and i. So: Bus stop 1. Then update, i is 2. [TRACK i=2] Check, print Bus stop 2. And so on up to Bus stop 5. When i becomes 6, the check fails and we leave. One small thing: because i was declared inside the for, it only exists inside that loop. Outside, i is gone. Second loop. [HL 8] int sum equals 0. Always start a total at zero. [TRACK sum=0] [HL 9] for, int n equals 1, n less than or equal to 10, n plus plus. [HL 10] sum equals sum plus n. Watch the tracker. n is 1, sum is 1. [TRACK n=1 sum=1] n is 2, sum is 3. [TRACK n=2 sum=3] n is 3, sum is 6. Then 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, and finally 55. [TRACK n=10 sum=55] [HL 12] Line twelve prints "Sum of 1 to 10 = 55". Third loop counts down. [HL 14] for, int t equals 3, t greater than or equal to 1, t minus minus. Start at 3, keep going while t is at least 1, and subtract one each time. [TRACK t=3] [HL 15] Print t, then three dots and a space, no newline. So we get 3, 2, 1 on the same line. [TRACK t=0] When t hits 0, the check fails. [HL 17] Then we print "Go!" and a newline.

scenes.narration: Why did the for loop always arrive on time? Because it planned everything in advance.

scenes.animation: Butter frame, a missing "10" box blinks Tomato; buzzer
scenes.narration: Today's bug: off-by-one. The task says print 1 to 10. A student writes: for int i equals 1, i less than 10, i plus plus. Compile: no error. Run: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9. Where is 10? When i is 10, is 10 less than 10? No. So the loop stops one step early. The fix: use less than or equal to 10. A quick check that always works: ask "what is the last value I want?" and test that value in your condition by hand.

scenes.onScreen: Two-column card: for = you know the count; while = you wait for a condition
scenes.animation: Cards flip, Mint tick on each example
scenes.narration: So when do you use which? If you know how many times, use for. Ten bus stops, fifty numbers, the length of a list. If you are waiting for something to happen, use while. Waiting until the fish count passes 100, or until the user types zero. Both can do the same job. Choose the one that makes your code easier to read.

shorts.title: One Line, Whole Plan
shorts.hook: Three scattered code lines snapping into one
shorts.script: This while loop needs three separate lines: start, check, update. The for loop puts all three in one line. for int i equals 1, i less than or equal to 50, i plus plus. Same job, cleaner code.
shorts.caption: Same loop, half the clutter.

shorts.title: The for Loop in 30 Seconds
shorts.hook: The for line split into START / CHECK / STEP
shorts.script: Three parts, two semicolons. Init runs once at the start. The condition is checked before every round. The update runs after every round. Init, check, body, update, check, body, update, until the check is false. That's the for loop.
shorts.caption: The for loop, decoded.

shorts.title: Where Did 10 Go?
shorts.hook: Output "1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9" with a blinking empty box
shorts.script: Task: print 1 to 10. Output: 1 to 9. Where did 10 go? The condition says i less than 10, and 10 is not less than 10. Off-by-one. Use less than or equal to, and always test your last value by hand.
shorts.caption: The off-by-one bug costs marks.

shorts.title: Pun: Always on Time
shorts.hook: Xecxec with a calendar and a watch
shorts.script: Why did the for loop always arrive on time? Because it planned everything in advance.
shorts.caption: The most organised loop in C.

shorts.title: How Many Times Does It Run?
shorts.script: Quiz. for int t equals 3, t greater than or equal to 1, t minus minus. How many times does the body run? Three. t is 3, then 2, then 1. At 0 the check fails. Did you say 4? Comment your answer.
shorts.caption: Count carefully.
